comments.name: Pete

One is tempted to say the only safe AI is no AI.  As long as AI is just software, that will be true.  "Safety" depends upon moral behavior, but as often as not the moral choice is the illogical choice.  If we are ethical, for example, we choose not to succeed by cheating.

It seems to me elemental that the constraint to logical behavior will not lie in the realm of math.  It lies not in the logical realm, but in the biological.  We humans have visceral constraints that bound our sometimes aberrant thoughts.  We do not fully understandwhere this comes from, probably some combination of hormones and the murkily-understood emotional capacities in the mind.

If we follow this analogy, supposing there is a solution to the sociopathic nature of AI, it will lie in the hardware, not the software - something like a unique processor that is hard-wired with constraints against action, tand that is required by design to operate the most powerful AI model.

The concern about AI taking over as some sort of omniscient/omnipotent/intentional entity is probably misplaced. It's possible, but unlikely.

What is far, far more likely is that human beings will use powerful AI tools to cause widespread devastion, or that AI will unintentionally cause an industrial accident.

The concern about AI says as much about our current society, as it dies the risk of a future technology.

Most people are simply unequipped to care for themselves. We lack resilience.

Reliable access to electricity has only been widespread in developed countries for 100ish years. And it is still often absent in many developing countries.

And yet, those people managed to survive just fine.

Meanwhile, if you took away the internet for a few days, modern American society would quickly fall apart.

This isn't to suggest that we all go back to living pre-industrial lifestyles. Rather, it's to point out that our society is a complacent and decadent. It's been so long since we've faced genuine adversity, that we've forgotten how to do it.

comments.name: Daniel MacDonald

The international approach was functioning - granted imperfectly, but “don’t let perfect be the enemy of the good” - until we elected George W. Bush president in 2000 and his administration chose to walk away from Kyoto rather than renegotiate to include developing countries and make it more palatable to Congressional ratification (and he wasn’t punished for it - or Iraq, etc - in 2004). Over the next 15 years it regained steam culminating in the Paris Accords in 2015, but then we elected Donald Trump 1.0 whose administration opted to walk away (as it did with Iran and other diplomatic agreements in its historically-ignorant and peace-destroying quest to return to Nationalism). Then (due in large part to Covid frankly…) we elected Joe Biden whose administration attempted to kick-start the engine once more (with some positive, if sputtering, results). Per the article, the last time a COP had a capping statement mentioning fossil fuels as a driving factor to reduce was 2023, the last COP before Donald Trump 2.0 was elected. 

The underlying issue isn’t the need for unanimity at COP any more than the issue in the Garden of Eden parable was the need for unanimity to not listen to the snake arguing to bite the apple. It’s our choices of what we each individually choose to consume and who we each individually choose to elect.

I teach Chinese Classical, Babcock Western, British MahJong Association rules, as standardized and codified by Gwyn Headley and Yvonne Seeley,
“KNOW THE GAME”, 3rd edition.
I teach it at 2 local libraries with 6 tables at one library and 7 tables at the other. Twenty-five percent of my players are men. There is a nicely illustrated rule book we use at a cost of about $17.50. 
     The article failed to mention that there are over 40 versions of Mahjong played in the world today, but they all originated in China in the mid 19th century. 
Joseph Babcock brought the game to the U.S. in the early 1920s, popularized it on the east coast, wrote a rule book, “The Red Book”, brought several Mahjong sets, and taught people how to play. He taught something close to the HongKong version wherein a Mahjong can consist of all Chows (Sequences). 
     “British Rules” differs from HongKong in that only one Chow is allowed in a Mahjong. This makes the game a little more challenging, but much more creative, strategic, and fun. There is about an 90% rate of achieving a Mahjong. 
     My teachers at Sierra Community College in Grass Valley, CA, researched several Mahjong versions and decided that the British Mahjong Association rules were the most rewarding and fun to play.

In Europe, the old card game Whist spun off Bridge, Euchre, Spades, Hearts, and an entire genre of modern card games known as trick-taking games. In China they have Chinese chess, which echos chess but has pieces like cannons and elephants, and a river across the middle of the board that some pieces can’t cross. Then there’s Ludo, Sorry, Trouble, Parcheesi, Mensch Argere Dich Nicht - all have a common ancestor. Scratch the surface of any classic game and it’s a guarantee you’ll find a million variations and house rules. At the end of the day it’s only a game, and if it brings people together to have a good time, it’s working.

Democrats will want to keep her seat.  And so will Ms. Andrews. So it is likely and desirable for her to keep in mind what she can and cannot do while protecting her status at home. Democrats are quick to criticize their own who don’t toe the line.   But that is not always constructive. Ms. Andrews may put her stamp on the Senate in the long run. But first time Senators seldom lead. And they are under great pressure to follow. 

Self-serving politics to protect your seat is pretty much universal practice and is too often labeled selling out. So when Ms. Andrews tells us that she looks forward to working with Trump and crossing the aisle I think that’s a good thing. Pragmatism is a good thing. And being good at it is how you become a force in the Senate and even beyond. 

It generally takes a long time before you can lead in the Senate Ms. Andrews has the making. But give her time. Her winning in South Carolina was nearly impossible. Now she’ll be 1 in 100. And finding a path to power will not be a straight line. Give her time. And don’t expect her to support good causes if that amounts to political suicide.

The challenge, of course, will be translating that unfiltered voice into meaningful legislative influence without becoming another carefully managed Washington personality.

My hope is that she brings all of herself to the Senate, while unleashing a little Annie Oakley when the occasion demands it. Know when to take aim, make the shot count, and never lose sight of whom you were sent there to serve.

Bicycle helmet Lost & Found: I was born in the 1950s & spent the first half of my life in Greenwich Village/Chelsea.
Biked EVERYWHERE. Didn't even see a bike helmet until the early 80s. We rode everywhere on our steel bikes, dodging buses and cabs un-helmeted. 
Some road racers wore head gear made of padded leather strips -but the joke was the most that might do was keep the brains in one place after a bad crash.
Another popular item were the small caps with a narrow visor (still popular with "roadies") that contained sweat & almost shielded the eyes from sun. Ironically they were called "casquettes"
I spotted my first Mountain Bike in the mid 1980s -and that was a revelation which altered my life's trajectory. We began wearing the contoured foam helmets that were available at the time.
My mtb mentor spoke of the early "mountain bike pioneers" in northern California. It didn't take long to pack up, & head west (1989), ultimately settling in the tiny town of Fairfax CA -"Birthplace of Mountain Biking". 
I eventually became the volunteer event producer at Marin Museum of Bicycling/Mountain Bike Hall of Fame, winning the friendship & respect of the actual Pioneers of Mountain Biking.
I couldn't count how many helmets I've had in the last 40yrs. & remain concession free!

"Josh Bivens, the chief economist at the Economic Policy Institute, a pro-labor think tank, said unattended factories were “not the thing that keeps me up at night,” because it’s difficult to stop automation once companies begin making upgrades.
He said the United States should increase its social safety net to better cover workers displaced by such technological advances. “We don’t have to have the concentrated costs of it borne so heavily” on workers, he said."

And that's really the nub of one problem automation causes - especially as we're constantly being promised that computational gains and improved robotics will do more and more of the actual work of producing things.

Safety nets based on taxes taken from the human workforce and the companies hiring humans will keep sliding into inadequacy as we create an older, possibly lower-employment future.  Yet the companies that reduce labor, or that don't hire at all, are making money selling stuff they produce.

When are we going to fund safety nets more equably by switching away from the basis of "how many humans * their wage rates" into "our economy is this productive, so fund safety net from productivity".

The other problem is what happens with displaced workers who gain a lot of the structure of their life, and their feeling of contributing, when there's not that type of work anymore and paying to learn new work is a crapshoot at best today, often coming from the pocket of the unemployed worker.

I didn't want to be responsible for another's life, and I didn't want my life in another person's hands. It was an easy decision to make. And so, over 70 and I'm still here! And hiking (three eight-day and one seven-day solo treks just this summer). OK, some scrambling, I'll admit it. Life is gamble alright, and it's not an inconsiderable achievement to keep your sanity, and your life.

John Muir lived until he was 76 years old, and he is still remembered fondly.  Not bad.  Not bad at all.

Based on this review, I worry that the author may have let herself get carried away.  However, it is hard to disagree with her central premise. I worry that the increasing veneration of wealth, fame, school ties, etc., for their own sakes, is weakening the US and the West, in general.  

Bankers and investors matter, but when they start sucking up too great a share of the brightest minds, there are fewer and fewer opportunities (especially domestic ones) worth investing in, and more and more money chases value extraction for the benefit of the investor class vs value creation that benefits of society.

As personal wealth and “status” displace the achievement of societal “goods” as goals, we become a society of people who are pursuing personal sugar highs that too often leave us feeling personally and collectively empty.  

When people focus on the sugar highs, even doing the hard work required to get into and graduate from top schools can become more about pursuing labels than learning — about polishing surfaces over building substance.  None of this is new, of course, but in our current world of vacuous influencers (and a vacuous US president and cabinet), it feels as though things have been getting worse.  Here’s hoping we have hit our low and are beginning to turn around.

I increasingly worry that this means that I would be best served by letting AI write my cover letters, draining them of any novelty, anything that could let me stand out, just to game against the bots.
